giai_thich: The immense heat of the fire causes the air to rise very strongly, carrying smoke, ash, and water vapor up to 10 km or more, creating a separate thunderstorm cloud. This cloud can produce lightning that ignites new areas, and gusts from it can change the direction of the fire unpredictably. During the 2019-2020 wildfire season in Australia, fire clouds even pushed smoke up to the stratosphere.

cau_hoi: In the dry lakebed of Racetrack Playa (Death Valley, USA), rocks weighing hundreds of kilograms seem to 'move' across the ground, leaving long trails. How did scientists explain this in 2014?
A: Thin ice sheets on shallow water are pushed by the wind, dragging the rocks along
B: Due to earthquakes making the rocks jump
C: Due to magnetic fields pulling the rocks
giai_thich: For decades, no one saw these rocks move. In 2014, a group of scientists set up cameras and attached GPS to the rocks. They discovered that in winter, when the lakebed is covered with a thin layer of water and freezes, the next morning the ice breaks into large sheets, the light wind pushes them, and they slide the rocks slowly across the slick mud, a few meters per minute.

cau_hoi: "Atmospheric river" is what?
A: A river flowing on top of high mountains
D: A long and narrow band of water vapor in the sky, capable of carrying more water than the Amazon River
giai_thich: An atmospheric river can be thousands of kilometers long but only a few hundred kilometers wide, transporting water vapor from the tropics. When it encounters mountains, the water vapor rises, condenses, and falls as heavy rain. Atmospheric rivers provide most of the rainfall for California (USA), but excessively strong bands can also cause severe flooding and landslides.

cau_hoi: "Polar vortex" is what, and why does it sometimes cause record cold spells in North America and Asia?
A: A hole in the Arctic ice
B: A tropical storm moving to the Arctic
C: A low-pressure area with strong swirling winds that keeps cold air around the poles; when it weakens, the cold air spills southward
giai_thich: Normally, westerly winds blow strongly around the poles like a barrier, trapping the extremely cold polar air in the Arctic region. When the polar vortex is disturbed and distorted, 'tongues' of cold air spill down to lower latitudes. In 2021, such a cold air outbreak caused Texas (USA) to freeze, leading to widespread power outages for several days.

cau_hoi: According to satellite measurements, how fast is the global average sea level currently rising?
giai_thich: Since 1993, satellite measurements of sea level have shown that the rate of rise has increased from about 2 mm to about 4 mm per year, indicating that it is accelerating. From 1900 to now, sea levels have risen by about 20 cm. In low-lying areas like the Mekong Delta, a few tens of centimeters of additional sea level rise can cause severe flooding and saltwater intrusion.

cau_hoi: Many giant salt mines lie deep underground, with layers hundreds of meters thick. How are they formed?
A: Ancient seas or isolated salt lakes, where water evaporates leaving salt, then buried
giai_thich: When a shallow sea is isolated from the ocean in a hot, dry climate, water evaporates quickly, salt crystallizes, and settles to the bottom. New seawater floods in and then evaporates again, repeating for thousands of years to create very thick salt layers. About 6 million years ago, the Mediterranean Sea nearly dried up, leaving a salt layer over 1 km thick beneath today's seabed.

cau_hoi: What characteristics does the "fossil" groundwater beneath the Sahara Desert, such as the Nubian sandstone aquifer, have?
A: It is water poured by humans
C: It was formed from last year's rain
D: It has been stored from thousands to millions of years ago when the climate was humid, and is almost not replenished
giai_thich: When the Sahara was green, rainwater seeped deep into the sandstone layers. Today, there is almost no rain to replenish it, so using this water is like withdrawing savings without any income. Libya has built the "Great Man-Made River" project with thousands of kilometers of pipelines to bring this groundwater to coastal cities.

cau_hoi: When cutting into a deep soil wall, we see different layers. The top layer of soil, dark and richest in humus, where most plant roots and earthworms live, is commonly referred to as what?
giai_thich: Soil scientists divide soil profiles into several layers: O layer is the top layer of decomposed leaves, A layer is the rich humus topsoil, B layer accumulates clay and minerals washed down from above, C layer is the weathering parent rock, and R layer is bedrock. The topsoil layer is only a few tens of centimeters thick but supports most of the world's crops.

cau_hoi: According to conventions in Vietnam, a tropical cyclone is called a "storm" (instead of a tropical depression) when the maximum wind speed near the center reaches what level or higher?
giai_thich: Tropical depressions have winds of levels 6-7. When the maximum wind speed reaches level 8 (about 62-74 km/h) or higher, it becomes a storm and is given an international name. Level 10-11 storms are strong storms, level 12-15 are very strong storms, and level 16 and above are super typhoons. In addition to the average wind level, meteorological stations also report "gusts", which are stronger winds for short periods.

cau_hoi: Flash floods, which cause significant damage in the northern mountainous regions of Vietnam, differ from regular river floods in what way?
B: Form and arrive very quickly after heavy rain in steep areas, carrying soil and rocks, almost without warning
giai_thich: In steep mountainous areas, when there is very heavy rain in a short time, water accumulates in narrow stream beds, creating extremely strong flows that carry mud, rocks, and trees, in just a few hours or less. Deforestation in upstream areas makes the soil unable to retain water, making flash floods more dangerous. In 2024, after Typhoon Yagi, flash floods buried the Nủ village (Lào Cai), causing significant damage.

cau_hoi: What transformations can a granite rock undergo in the "rock cycle"?
D: Weathered into sand, compressed into sandstone, then transformed into metamorphic rock by heat and pressure
giai_thich: Granite exposed to the surface is broken down by sun and rain, and quartz grains wash into the sea as sand. Sand is buried and compressed into sandstone (sedimentary rock). When buried deeper, sandstone is subjected to heat and pressure, transforming into quartzite (metamorphic rock). If melted, it becomes magma and can cool into new granite. This cycle takes hundreds of millions of years and was described by geologist James Hutton in the 18th century.

cau_hoi: Clouds that look like rolling sea waves in the sky are called Kelvin-Helmholtz clouds. When do they form?
B: When the Moon is close to Earth
C: When two layers of air slide past each other at different speeds, with the upper layer moving faster
giai_thich: Just as wind blowing across a lake creates waves, when the upper layer of air moves faster than the lower layer, the boundary between them rolls up into waves. If there are clouds at the boundary, we see those waves. They only last a few minutes. Some believe these clouds inspired the swirling sky in Van Gogh's painting "Starry Night."

cau_hoi: Mammatus clouds, which look like round bags hanging down from the base of clouds, typically appear where?
C: Under the anvil of large thunderstorm clouds
giai_thich: Mammatus clouds form when cold air, containing a lot of ice and water, sinks from the base of a thunderstorm cloud, unlike most clouds that form from rising air. The name comes from the Latin word "mamma" (breast). They look ominous and are often associated with severe thunderstorms, but they are not dangerous themselves.

cau_hoi: "Green flash" is a rare phenomenon that occurs when?
A: In the middle of a scorching noon
B: Right as the Sun sets or rises on a clear horizon, like the sea surface
D: When there is a double rainbow
giai_thich: The atmosphere bends the light of different colors slightly, with green light bending more than red light. Therefore, when the Sun's disk is almost completely hidden, the top part can flash green for a second or two. This phenomenon requires a very distant horizon and very clear air. The writer Jules Verne even wrote a novel titled "The Green Flash" in 1882.

cau_hoi: The "lake-effect snow" phenomenon causes cities near the Great Lakes (North America) to experience very heavy snowfall. How does it occur?
A: Ice from the lake rises into the sky
B: The lake's surface reflects causing more snow to fall
C: Winds carry snow directly from the Arctic
D: Cold air blows over the still-warm lake, picking up moisture and then depositing it as snow on the opposite shore
giai_thich: At the beginning of winter, the lake water is still much warmer than the air. When a stream of extremely cold, dry air blows over the lake surface, it warms up and picks up additional moisture, creating cloud bands. Upon reaching the shore, especially when encountering high hills, the clouds dump very heavy snow over a narrow area. In 2014, the city of Buffalo (New York) experienced snow depths of about 2 meters in just a few days.

cau_hoi: "Banded iron formation" (BIF), rocks with red stripes of iron oxide alternating with gray stripes, mostly formed about 2.5 – 1.8 billion years ago, record what event?
A: Oxygen produced by photosynthetic bacteria began to accumulate, causing dissolved iron in the sea to oxidize and precipitate
D: Earth was completely covered in ice for the first time
giai_thich: Ancient seas contained a lot of dissolved iron. When cyanobacteria began to release oxygen, iron combined with oxygen to form insoluble iron oxide, sinking to the bottom and forming iron-rich layers. Most of the world's iron ore today, such as in Australia and Brazil, comes from these banded iron layers. After the iron in the sea was "used up," oxygen could then accumulate in the atmosphere.

cau_hoi: The phenomenon of water in a lake or bay oscillating back and forth like water sloshing in a basin, after strong winds or sudden changes in pressure, is called what?
giai_thich: When strong winds blow water to one end of a lake and then suddenly stop, the water sloshes back and forth multiple times, like when you carry a basin of water. In Lake Erie (North America), seiche can cause the water level at both ends to differ by several meters. In 2011, an earthquake in Japan even created seiche in narrow fjords in Norway, thousands of kilometers away.

cau_hoi: How has the Arctic sea ice extent at the end of summer (September) changed since satellite measurements began in 1979?
B: Reduced by about 40%, with a record low in 2012
giai_thich: In September 2012, Arctic sea ice was only about 3.4 million km², the lowest since satellite monitoring began, compared to about 7 million km² at the end of the 1970s. The ice has not only shrunk but also thinned significantly. Scientists predict that the Arctic could have summers with almost no ice by 2050.

cau_hoi: "Wilson cycle" in geology describes what process that repeats over hundreds of millions of years?
A: An ocean opens as continents drift apart, then closes as continents collide
C: Sea levels rise and fall with tides
giai_thich: Canadian geologist John Tuzo Wilson recognized that rocks on both sides of the Atlantic Ocean once belonged to an ancient mountain range. A continent is torn apart (like East Africa today), the sea floods in, the ocean widens (like the Atlantic), then the ocean floor is subducted, the ocean shrinks, and continents collide to form mountains (like the Himalayas). Each cycle lasts about 300 – 500 million years.

cau_hoi: "South Atlantic Anomaly" is a region where Earth's magnetic field has what characteristic, causing problems for satellites and the Hubble telescope?
A: Magnetic field is a hundred times stronger
C: Unusually weak magnetic field, allowing radiation particles to come closer to Earth
giai_thich: This region extends from South America to southern Africa. Due to the weak magnetic field, the Van Allen radiation belt is lower, allowing high-energy particles to cause computer malfunctions on satellites. The Hubble telescope has to turn off some instruments whenever it flies through, and astronauts on the International Space Station sometimes see flashes in their eyes when passing through this area. The anomaly region is expanding and splitting in two.

cau_hoi: Which Scottish geologist, in the 18th century, is considered the "father of modern geology" with the famous remark that the Earth "has no trace of a beginning, nor any prospect of an end"?
giai_thich: Hutton observed rock layers at Siccar Point (Scotland): horizontal sedimentary rocks overlaid on vertical layers below. He understood that it took an extremely long time for the underlying rock to form, be tilted, eroded, and then the upper layer to deposit. This idea of "deep time", along with the principle that processes occurring today also happened in the past, laid the foundation for geology.

cau_hoi: In 1815, who published the first geological map showing the rock layers of an entire country (England, Wales, and part of Scotland)?
giai_thich: William Smith was a surveyor working in coal mines and canals. He realized that each rock layer contained its own fossils and that the layers were always arranged in the same order. His map, about 2.6 meters long, was called the "map that changed the world". However, due to his humble background, he was looked down upon by the scientific community, his ideas were copied, and he was once imprisoned for debt.

cau_hoi: In 1962, which American geologist proposed an important idea that helped explain continental drift?
C: Continents drift on the ocean surface
D: New ocean floor is created at mid-ocean ridges and spreads outwards
giai_thich: During World War II, Hess served as a naval captain and used sonar depth gauges on his ship to record the ocean floor. After the war, he proposed that magma rises at mid-ocean ridges, creating new ocean floor and pushing the old floor apart like a conveyor belt, sinking at deep trenches. This "sea floor spreading" idea addressed the question of the force that Wegener could not answer.

cau_hoi: What significant contribution did female scientist Marie Tharp make to Earth science in the 1950s?
B: Mapped the ocean floor, discovering the rift valley running along the mid-Atlantic ridge
giai_thich: At that time, women were not allowed on survey ships, so Tharp worked in a laboratory drawing maps from thousands of depth measurements. She discovered a deep rift running along the ridge's peak, evidence that the ocean floor was being pulled apart. Her colleagues initially dismissed it, calling it "girl talk". Her and Bruce Heezen's world ocean floor map from 1977 became very famous.

cau_hoi: In addition to P-waves and S-waves that travel through the Earth, earthquakes also generate surface waves that typically cause the most damage. What are these waves?
giai_thich: Surface waves arrive after P and S waves but have larger amplitudes and longer durations, causing the most damage. Love waves (named after mathematician Augustus Love) make the ground shake side to side like a snake. Rayleigh waves (named after Lord Rayleigh) cause the ground to move in rolling circles like ocean waves. At a distance from the epicenter, people can sometimes see the ground ripple.

cau_hoi: "Hadley Cell", named after George Hadley (1735), describes what movement of air?
A: Winds blowing down from mountains into valleys at night
C: Warm air rises at the equator, moves towards the poles at high altitudes, descends at about 30° latitude, and then returns to the equator near the ground
D: Air swirling in the eye of a storm
giai_thich: The Hadley Cell explains many phenomena: heavy rainfall at the equator where air rises, large deserts around 30° latitude where dry air descends, and trade winds blowing towards the equator. Hadley was an English lawyer passionate about meteorology. In addition to the Hadley Cell, each hemisphere also has the Ferrel Cell at mid-latitudes and the polar cell near the poles.

cau_hoi: According to physical laws, each time the temperature increases by 1°C, how much more water vapor can the air hold?
giai_thich: This relationship is derived from the Clausius – Clapeyron equation. Therefore, as the Earth warms, the air holds more water vapor, and when it rains, it can rain harder, causing more flooding. At the same time, water vapor is also a greenhouse gas, which further warms the Earth. This is why climate change makes both droughts and heavy rains more severe.

cau_hoi: In terms of heat retention, which greenhouse gas contributes the most to Earth's natural greenhouse effect?
giai_thich: Water vapor contributes about half of the natural greenhouse effect, clouds add a significant portion, while CO₂ accounts for about 20%. However, the amount of water vapor in the air depends on temperature: if more water vapor is added, it will rain down in a few days. CO₂, on the other hand, lasts for hundreds of years, making it like a "thermostat" for temperature, and water vapor amplifies its effect.

cau_hoi: In the ocean, the layer of water between the warm surface layer and the cold deep layer, where the temperature drops rapidly with depth, is called what?
giai_thich: The surface layer is warmed by the Sun and mixed by wind, while the deep water below is cold at about 0 – 4°C. In the thermocline, the temperature can drop several degrees within just a few dozen meters. This layer hinders water exchange, making it difficult for nutrients from below to rise to the surface. Submarines also take advantage of the thermocline to hide because it bends sonar sound waves.

cau_hoi: "Methane hydrate" at the ocean floor is what?
C: Ice containing trapped methane gas, which can catch fire
giai_thich: At the cold and high-pressure ocean floor, water molecules form crystalline cages trapping methane gas inside, looking like ice but can catch fire when ignited. The amount of methane in methane hydrates on Earth is estimated to be very large, potentially a future energy source. However, if the oceans warm and the hydrates melt, the released methane could further warm the climate.

cau_hoi: In the Himalayas, when glaciers melt rapidly, glacial lakes form behind the earth and rock dams left by the glaciers. What is the greatest danger from these lakes?
D: The earth and rock dam can suddenly break, causing massive floods down the valley
giai_thich: The glacial dams are made from loose, unstable earth and rock. A glacier collapse or earthquake can cause water to overflow and break the dam, releasing millions of cubic meters of water in a few hours. Glacial lake outburst floods have destroyed many villages in Nepal, Bhutan, and India, such as the flood in 2013 in Kedarnath and in 2023 in Sikkim. Climate change is rapidly increasing the number and size of these lakes.

cau_hoi: The Thwaites Glacier in West Antarctica, nearly the size of England, has a frightening nickname. What is it?
giai_thich: Thwaites contains enough ice to raise global sea levels by about 65 cm if it melts completely. Its base is being eroded from below by warmer seawater, and it acts as a "block" holding back larger ice masses behind it. If Thwaites collapses, the entire West Antarctic ice sheet could slide into the sea more rapidly. Scientists have drilled through the ice to place measuring devices beneath it.

cau_hoi: How is laterite, the type of stone used for building houses in the ancient village of Duong Lam, formed?
A: Soil in humid tropical regions is washed away, with iron and aluminum accumulating and hardening when dry
giai_thich: In heavily rainy tropical regions, rainwater washes away most soluble minerals, leaving only iron and aluminum oxides. This layer of soil is soft when moist and can be cut into blocks, but when exposed to air, it dries and hardens like stone, with a reddish-brown color and many holes like a beehive. The term "laterite" comes from the Latin word "later" meaning brick. The Angkor Wat temple also used laterite as its core.

cau_hoi: What is a sandbar that connects an island to the mainland, formed by wave deposition, called?
giai_thich: When waves circle around both sides of an island near the shore, they converge at the back of the island, slowing the water down and allowing sand to settle, gradually connecting the island to the mainland. Many tombolos are only exposed at low tide, like the path to the former Mont-Saint-Michel monastery in France. The name comes from Italian, meaning "sandbank".

cau_hoi: What are crescent-shaped sand dunes, with two pointed tips facing the wind, that move quite quickly across the desert called?
giai_thich: Barchan dunes form in areas with wind blowing mainly from one direction and not too much sand. The wind pushes sand up the windward slope, and then the sand falls down the leeward slope. The tips on both sides are lower and have less sand, so they move faster than the middle part, creating a crescent shape. Some barchan dunes can move tens of meters each year and can bury roads and houses. Barchan dunes are also found on Mars.

cau_hoi: What surprising commonality do emeralds and aquamarines share?
C: Both are beryl minerals, differing only by a very small amount of impurities
giai_thich: Beryl is colorless in its pure form. When it contains a little chromium or vanadium, it turns dark green to become emerald; when it contains a little iron, it turns blue to become aquamarine. The same occurs with rubies and sapphires, which are both corundum minerals. Just a few foreign atoms among millions of atoms are enough to change the color of the gemstone.

cau_hoi: What mineral gives the olive green color of the sand at Papakōlea beach (Hawaii)?
giai_thich: Olivine is a mineral rich in magnesium and iron, making up a large part of the Earth's upper mantle. At Papakōlea, ocean waves break down an ancient volcanic crater containing many olivine crystals; olivine is heavier than other grains, so it stays on the beach, creating the rare green sand. Gem-quality olivine is called peridot. Olivine is also found in meteorites and on the Moon and Mars.

cau_hoi: Where does the name of the Cambrian period, the "explosion of life" period about 538 – 485 million years ago, originate from?
A: From "Cambria", the Latin name for Wales, where rocks from this period were first studied
D: From the name of a scientist
giai_thich: Geologist Adam Sedgwick named the Cambrian period in 1835 while studying rocks in northern Wales. Many other geological periods are also named after places or peoples: the Ordovician and Silurian periods after ancient tribes in Wales, the Devonian after the county of Devon in England, the Permian after the Perm region in Russia, and the Jurassic after the Jura Mountains between France and Switzerland.

cau_hoi: What do seismologists mean by the term "seismic gap"?
A: A void in the Earth's core
B: A segment of a fault that has not experienced a major earthquake for a long time, and may be accumulating energy
C: A region that never experiences earthquakes
D: The time interval between P waves and S waves
giai_thich: Along a long fault, segments take turns "slipping" during major earthquakes. If there is a segment that has been quiet for a long time while both sides have slipped, that segment may be stuck and accumulating stress. In 1989, an earthquake in California occurred right at such a seismic gap. However, this method only indicates where there is a high risk, not predicting the exact timing.

cau_hoi: Since around 2009, Oklahoma (USA), which rarely experiences earthquakes, suddenly has hundreds of earthquakes each year. What is the main identified cause?
A: The Moon coming closer to Earth
D: Pumping large amounts of wastewater from oil and gas extraction deep underground
giai_thich: Saline wastewater that accompanies oil and gas extraction is pumped into deep rock layers. The water increases pressure in the fractures of old faults, acting like lubrication, making them easier to slip and causing earthquakes. In 2016, a 5.8 magnitude earthquake occurred in Oklahoma. After the state restricted wastewater pumping, the number of earthquakes decreased significantly. This is an example of "human-induced earthquakes."

cau_hoi: Above strong thunderstorm clouds, red jellyfish-shaped flashes of light sometimes appear, reaching heights of about 90 km. What are they called?
giai_thich: Sprites are electrical phenomena that occur in the mesosphere, just after a strong lightning strike, lasting only a few milliseconds. Pilots have reported seeing them, but they were not recorded until 1989 by chance using a camera. In addition to sprites, there are 'blue jets' that shoot up from the tops of clouds and 'elves', which are expanding red rings of light. Astronauts on the International Space Station have captured many sprites.

cau_hoi: Outside the atmosphere, how much energy does each square meter perpendicular to sunlight receive from the Sun each second?
giai_thich: This number is called the 'solar constant', although it changes slightly according to the solar activity cycle. By the time it reaches the ground, after being absorbed and reflected by the atmosphere, only about 1,000 W/m² remains at noon on a clear day. For the entire Earth, the solar energy received in about one hour is enough for all humanity to use for a year.

cau_hoi: On average, what percentage of sunlight that reaches the Earth is reflected back into space?
giai_thich: The average reflectivity (albedo) of the Earth is about 0.3, mainly due to clouds, ice, and partly due to land. About 70% of the remaining energy is absorbed, warming the land, water, and air. If ice melts and clouds change, this ratio also changes, affecting the climate. The Moon is much darker, reflecting only about 12%, similar to old coal.

cau_hoi: To 'seed clouds' for artificial rain, what substance is typically sprinkled into the clouds?
giai_thich: Silver iodide crystals have a structure very similar to ice crystals, so water vapor and supercooled water droplets in the clouds adhere to them and freeze around them, creating ice particles heavy enough to fall. This method was developed by Vincent Schaefer and Bernard Vonnegut in 1946-1947. However, cloud seeding is only effective when suitable clouds are present, and its actual effectiveness is still debated.

cau_hoi: What UV index is classified as 'very high', indicating that sun exposure should be limited during midday?
giai_thich: The higher the UV index, the faster the skin burns: 0 – 2 low, 3 – 5 moderate, 6 – 7 high, 8 – 10 very high, and 11 and above extremely high. In Vietnam during summer noon, the UV index often reaches levels of 10 – 12, with some places higher. UV rays can still penetrate thin clouds, so overcast skies can still lead to sunburn. Wide-brimmed hats, long-sleeved shirts, and sunscreen help protect the skin.

cau_hoi: Where is the densest and deepest body of water in the world's oceans formed?
A: At the mouths of large rivers
B: In tropical seas around the equator
D: Around Antarctica, where very cold and salty seawater sinks
giai_thich: When seawater around Antarctica freezes, salt is pushed out of the ice, making the surrounding water both very cold and saltier, thus very dense. It sinks to the bottom and flows slowly northward along the ocean floor, known as Antarctic bottom water. This body of water extends to the North Atlantic and Pacific Oceans, helping to deliver oxygen to the deepest parts of the ocean.

cau_hoi: In 2023, scientists published a notable study about the Earth's inner core. What did they suggest might have happened?
A: The inner core has completely melted
B: The inner core has stopped rotating permanently and the Earth will stop
C: The inner core is temporarily rotating slower than the crust, possibly in cycles of several decades
D: The inner core has fallen out of the Earth's center
giai_thich: The inner core is separated from the mantle by the outer liquid core, so it can rotate slightly faster or slower than the rest. By comparing waves from repeating earthquakes at the same location over decades, scientists inferred this change. This is an extremely small change, only altering the length of a day by about a millisecond, and is not dangerous.

cau_hoi: What was the 'Laschamp event' about 41,000 years ago?
A: The formation of the South China Sea
B: A period of significant weakening of the Earth's magnetic field and temporary pole reversal lasting several hundred years
giai_thich: During this event, the Earth's magnetic field was at times weaker than 10% of today's strength, then reversed over several hundred years before returning to normal. Scientists found traces in the lava flow in the village of Laschamp (France). When the magnetic field was weak, more cosmic rays reached the Earth, leaving traces of special isotopes in ice cores and ancient wood.

cau_hoi: The Hawaii – Emperor seamount chain at the bottom of the Pacific Ocean has a distinct bend. What does this bend indicate?
A: About 47 million years ago, the Pacific Plate changed its direction of movement (or the hotspot shifted)
B: The mountain chain was created by two different hotspots
C: Whales pulled the mountain chain off course
D: An earthquake bent the mountain chain
giai_thich: The Hawaii hotspot has created continuous volcanism for about 80 million years, leaving a seamount chain about 6,000 km long like a pen mark on the ocean floor. The older part (Emperor chain) runs north, while the newer part (Hawaii chain) runs northwest. Initially, it was thought that the plate changed direction, but later studies showed that the hotspot may have drifted as well, so this remains a topic of debate.

cau_hoi: The Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty Organization (CTBTO) uses a network of hundreds of stations worldwide, including seismometers, for what purpose?
giai_thich: An underground nuclear explosion generates seismic waves similar to a small earthquake, but with different characteristics: the source is very shallow, sudden, and produces more P-waves than S-waves. The network also includes infrasound stations, underwater hydrophones, and radiation measurement stations in the atmosphere. The data from the network also helps scientists study earthquakes and provide tsunami warnings.

cau_hoi: AMOC, a major ocean current system in the Atlantic that brings warm water north (including the Gulf Stream), is causing scientists concern for what reason?
B: It shows signs of weakening, and if it collapses, it could make Northern Europe much colder and change rainfall in many places
C: It has changed direction towards Antarctica
D: It is flowing ten times faster
giai_thich: Melting Greenland ice adds fresh, lighter water to the North Atlantic, making it harder for surface water to sink, weakening the 'pump' of the ocean current system. Many studies show that AMOC is at its weakest in about 1,600 years. Scientists consider this a 'tipping point' for the climate system: once crossed, it is very difficult to return.

cau_hoi: "Ensemble forecasting" used by meteorological agencies daily is what?
B: Using a very powerful computer to run once
D: Running the forecast model multiple times with slightly different initial data to see possible outcomes
giai_thich: Because the atmosphere is very sensitive to small initial errors, a single model run can yield incorrect results. Meteorological agencies run the model about 50 times, each time slightly changing the initial data. If the results are similar, the forecast is reliable; if they diverge in many directions, the forecast is less certain. The forecast path of storms shown in the news is built this way.

cau_hoi: The phenomenon of "cloud iridescence", where thin cloud edges have patches of pink and blue like mother-of-pearl, is caused by what?
C: Light diffracting through very uniformly sized small water droplets
giai_thich: When light passes through very small and uniform water droplets or ice crystals, it bends around the droplets (diffraction) and the colors separate. This phenomenon is often seen at the edges of newly formed clouds near the Sun, where the water droplets are still small and uniform. Unlike rainbows, which are always opposite the Sun, iridescent clouds appear near the Sun, so sunglasses should be worn and one should not look directly at the Sun when observing.

cau_hoi: "Brocken spectre" is what phenomenon that mountain climbers sometimes see?
A: The shadow of oneself cast large on the cloud below, with a colorful halo around the head
B: A strange animal on the mountain
giai_thich: When the Sun is behind and there are clouds or fog in front, a person's shadow cast on the clouds appears very large and seems to move. Around the head's shadow, colorful rings appear called 'glory', due to light being reflected back by small water droplets. The phenomenon is named after the Brocken peak in Germany. Airplane passengers sometimes also see the airplane's shadow with a similar colored ring on the clouds.

cau_hoi: In 2024, scientists announced a controversial discovery about metallic nodules on the bottom of the Pacific Ocean. What are they?
A: They are meteorites that fell recently
B: They can produce oxygen in the dark seabed without photosynthesis ('dark oxygen')
D: They are eggs of a strange organism
giai_thich: At a depth of about 4,000 meters, where there is no light, scientists measured an increase in oxygen instead of a decrease. They believe that nodules containing manganese, nickel, and cobalt can generate small electric currents sufficient to split water into oxygen and hydrogen. This discovery is still being verified but raises concerns about mining these nodules for metals to make batteries.

cau_hoi: Low hills shaped like elongated droplets, aligned in the same direction, commonly found in areas once covered by glaciers like Ireland or Canada, are called what?
giai_thich: Drumlin is formed when a thick layer of ice slides over and molds the underlying soil and rock into elongated hills. The steep and blunt end of the hill faces the direction from which the ice came, while the gentle and pointed end faces the direction the ice is moving. This allows geologists to know the direction the ancient ice sheet slid. Fields of drumlins can consist of thousands of hills resembling an upside-down egg carton.

cau_hoi: On the surface of glaciers, melting water can carve deep vertical wells hundreds of meters deep, pouring water down to the bottom of the glacier. What are they called?
giai_thich: Water melts in the summer and flows as streams on the surface of the ice, then when it encounters a crack, it pours down, gradually carving a deep swirling well. Water reaching the bottom makes the interface between ice and rock 'slippery', causing the glacier to slide faster. The term 'moulin' in French means 'mill', because the sound of the water pouring is like that of a water mill. Scientists have dropped devices and even rubber ducks into glacial wells to monitor the water flow.

cau_hoi: Cliffs with countless small round holes like a beehive or Swiss cheese, commonly found on coastlines and deserts, are called what?
giai_thich: Salt from seawater or groundwater seeps into the rock. When the water evaporates, salt crystallizes in the small holes, expanding and breaking down mineral grains. The small holes gradually grow larger because the inside is more humid and shaded, allowing salt to continue crystallizing. The name comes from the Corsican language (French), meaning 'window'. Tafoni has also been found on Mars.

cau_hoi: During large volcanic eruptions, lightning is often seen flashing within the ash column. What is the main cause?
B: Ash particles, debris, and ice colliding and rubbing against each other generating electric charges
C: The magnetic field of the volcano
giai_thich: In the violently rising ash column, billions of ash particles, rock fragments, and ice crystals (high up) collide, rub against each other, and break apart, generating opposite electric charges like when rubbing a balloon on hair. The electric charges separate in different parts of the ash column and then discharge as lightning. Volcanic lightning is particularly intense during the Hunga Tonga eruption in 2022, with about 400,000 lightning strikes recorded.

cau_hoi: Which mineral is considered the most abundant throughout the Earth, located in the lower mantle, but was only first found in natural samples in 2014 in a meteorite?
giai_thich: Bridgmanite makes up about 38% of the Earth's volume, but is only stable under extremely high pressure at depths of 660 – 2,700 km. When brought to the surface, it transforms into other minerals. Scientists have only found small crystals of it in the Tenham meteorite, where cosmic impacts created similar pressure. The name is given in honor of physicist Percy Bridgman, who won a Nobel Prize for research on high pressure.

cau_hoi: In 2001, in the state of Kerala (India), there were "red rains" that lasted for several weeks. What was later determined to be the cause?
B: Spores of a type of algae carried by the wind and falling with the rain
giai_thich: The rain appeared red like blood, causing panic among the locals. Some scientists initially suggested that the red particles were living cells from extraterrestrial sources from a meteorite, but later analysis showed they were spores of the green algae Trentepohlia, which grows abundantly on tree trunks and rooftops in the area. Colored rain can also occur when winds carry red dust from deserts.

cau_hoi: The Jakobshavn Glacier (Sermeq Kujalleq) in Greenland has been recorded as one of the fastest flowing glaciers in the world. In the summer of 2012, how fast did it flow?
giai_thich: Most glaciers only slide a few tens of centimeters to a few meters each day. Jakobshavn drains into the Ilulissat Bay, and it is believed that it produced the iceberg that sank the Titanic in 1912. The speed of the glacier varies with sea temperature; around 2016-2017, when colder water was present, it temporarily slowed down.

cau_hoi: How did Alfred Wegener, the father of the continental drift theory, die in 1930?
C: During an expedition on the Greenland ice sheet
giai_thich: Wegener was not only a meteorologist but also a polar explorer. In November 1930, after delivering supplies to a research station in the middle of the Greenland ice sheet, he set out to return during the harsh winter and never made it back; his body was found the following year. He died while his theory was still largely rejected by geologists.

cau_hoi: In 1692, astronomer Edmond Halley proposed a strange hypothesis about the structure of the Earth to explain the changing magnetic field. What was it?
A: The Earth has a giant magnet at the North Pole
B: The Earth is made of ice
C: The Earth is flat like a disk
D: The Earth is hollow, consisting of multiple concentric shells
giai_thich: Halley observed that the compass direction gradually changed over the years, so he theorized that inside the Earth there were concentric shells, each with its own magnetic pole and rotating at different speeds. He also suggested that the aurora borealis was gas escaping from inside. The "hollow Earth" hypothesis later inspired many works of fiction, such as Jules Verne's "Journey to the Center of the Earth."

cau_hoi: According to Buys Ballot's law in the Northern Hemisphere, if you stand with your back to the incoming wind, where will the low-pressure area be located?
giai_thich: In 1857, Dutch meteorologist C.H.D. Buys Ballot stated this law. Due to the Earth's rotation, winds do not blow directly into low-pressure areas but spiral around them, counterclockwise in the Northern Hemisphere. Therefore, with your back to the wind, the low-pressure area is to your left, slightly ahead. Sailors use this law to estimate the position of storm centers and steer their ships away. In the Southern Hemisphere, it is the opposite.

cau_hoi: "Fujiwhara effect" occurs when?
B: A storm encounters a cold ocean current
C: A storm makes landfall on high mountains
D: Two storms come close together and begin to rotate around a common point, sometimes merging into one
giai_thich: Japanese meteorologist Sakuhei Fujiwhara described this phenomenon in 1921 while studying whirlpools. When two storms are within about 1,400 km of each other, they influence each other's paths, can "dance" around each other, with the stronger storm swallowing the weaker one, or both suddenly changing direction. This makes forecasting storm paths more difficult.

cau_hoi: "Rapid intensification" of a tropical storm is defined as when, and why is it dangerous?
A: The storm lasts more than a month
B: The maximum wind speed increases by at least about 55 km/h in 24 hours, leaving people unprepared
D: The storm moves twice as fast
giai_thich: When a storm passes over very warm waters, with high humidity and weak upper-level winds, it can intensify from a weak storm to a superstorm in just one or two days. This is the most difficult scenario to predict. In 2023, Hurricane Otis in Mexico intensified by about 175 km/h in 24 hours before making landfall in Acapulco. Warmer sea temperatures due to climate change are causing this phenomenon to occur more frequently.

cau_hoi: Not only the sea, but the solid crust of the Earth also "rises and falls" according to the gravitational pull of the Moon and the Sun. How much can the ground rise each day?
giai_thich: This phenomenon is called Earth's tide (solid tide). Because a large area rises and falls together, we cannot perceive it. However, precise instruments must account for it: for example, the LHC particle accelerator in Europe, which is 27 km long, experiences a circumference change of about 1 mm due to the tide, affecting the measurable energy of the particle beam.

cau_hoi: On a glacier, sometimes the ice suddenly slides 10 to 100 times faster than normal for several months to years, then slows down again. What is this phenomenon called?
giai_thich: About 1% of glaciers worldwide experience this phenomenon. Ice accumulates gradually at the upper part for many years, until the water at the bottom is held back, making the base smoother, causing the entire mass of ice to suddenly slide down. In 1953, the Kutiah Glacier in Pakistan slid about 12 km in 3 months, with some days exceeding 100 m, considered one of the fastest recorded slides.

cau_hoi: About 8,200 years ago, a massive underwater landslide off the coast of Norway, known as the Storegga slide, caused what consequence?
C: A large tsunami flooded the coasts of Scotland, Norway, and the Doggerland region
giai_thich: A sediment block of about 3,000 km³ slid down the Norwegian continental shelf, possibly due to melting ice or an earthquake. The tsunami left a layer of marine sand deep inland in Scotland, in some places several meters above ancient sea level, and may have devastated Doggerland, the low-lying land connecting England to mainland Europe, now submerged under the North Sea.

cau_hoi: In lakes near glaciers, each year the lake bottom deposits a pair of sediment layers: a light coarse layer in summer and a dark fine layer in winter. What are these pairs of layers called, and what do scientists use them for?
A: Wood grain, to measure tree age
D: Varve, to count years and study past climates
giai_thich: In summer, melting glacier water carries coarse sand into the lake; in winter, the lake freezes, allowing only fine silt to settle slowly. Counting each pair of layers is like counting tree rings. In 1910, Swedish geologist Gerard De Geer used varves to date approximately 12,000 years, one of the first accurate dating methods in Earth science.

cau_hoi: In spring 2020, what did scientists unexpectedly discover in the ozone layer above the Arctic?
A: An unusually large ozone hole, rarely occurring in the Arctic
D: The ozone layer being twice as thick as normal
giai_thich: Ozone holes typically occur in Antarctica due to strong polar vortexes and extremely cold stratosphere, creating ice clouds that facilitate ozone-depleting substances. In 2020, an unusually strong and cold Arctic polar vortex persisted into spring, leading to significant ozone depletion, creating the largest hole ever recorded in the Arctic. The hole closed in April as the polar vortex dissipated.

cau_hoi: "Hair ice," delicate, white strands of ice that grow from decaying wood branches on damp, chilly nights, is formed by what?
B: A type of fungus living in wood that helps water freeze into fine strands
giai_thich: Hair ice only grows on dead broadleaf wood when temperatures are slightly below 0°C and the air is humid. In 1918, scientist Alfred Wegener (father of the continental drift theory) hypothesized a type of fungus was involved. In 2015, scientists confirmed that the fungus Exidiopsis effusa produces a substance that helps water freeze into fine strands of about 0.01 mm, maintaining their shape for hours.

cau_hoi: "Pingo" in permafrost regions like Canada and Siberia is what?
C: A hill with an ice core that gradually rises as groundwater freezes and expands
giai_thich: When a small lake in the tundra dries up, the groundwater below gradually freezes, expands, and pushes the overlying soil into a conical hill that can reach heights of 50 to 70 meters. The Tuktoyaktuk Peninsula in Canada has about 1,350 pingos, the most in the world. The name comes from the Inuvialuit word meaning "small hill." As the climate warms, the ice core melts and the pingo collapses into a depression.

cau_hoi: Deep beneath the mantle layer, below Africa and the Pacific Ocean, there are two massive blocks through which seismic waves pass slower than normal. A hypothesis that gained attention in 2023 suggests they could be what?
A: Remnants of Theia, the planet that collided with Earth and created the Moon
D: Two pieces of Earth's core that have broken apart
giai_thich: These blocks are called "large low shear velocity provinces" (LLSVP), each larger than a continent and hundreds of kilometers high. A research group simulated the collision that created the Moon about 4.5 billion years ago and suggested that a portion of Theia's iron-rich mantle sank down and still exists there. The hypothesis is still debated but indicates that the Earth's interior may retain traces from its primordial past.

cau_hoi: "Slow slip events," discovered around the year 2000 thanks to GPS networks, have what characteristics?
B: Seismic waves travel slower than sound
C: Earthquakes occur an hour later than predicted
D: Faults slip slowly over days to months, releasing large amounts of energy that humans cannot perceive
giai_thich: In some subduction zones like Cascadia (North America), Japan, and New Zealand, GPS stations detect the ground moving a few centimeters in the opposite direction over several weeks, like a large earthquake but occurring "slowly." The energy can be equivalent to a 6-7 magnitude earthquake. Scientists are researching whether slow earthquakes increase the risk of real large earthquakes occurring nearby.

cau_hoi: The earthquake accompanied by a tsunami and fire that destroyed the city of Lisbon (Portugal) in 1755 had a significant impact on which field besides geology?
B: European philosophy, leading many like Voltaire to question the belief that "everything is for the best"
giai_thich: The disaster occurred on All Saints' Day, when many people were in church, resulting in tens of thousands of deaths. Voltaire wrote a poem about the disaster and the novel "Candide" satirizing the optimistic notion that this is "the best of all possible worlds." The Portuguese Prime Minister Pombal sent out questionnaires across the country to gather information about the earthquake, considered the beginning of modern seismology.

cau_hoi: Which supercontinent existed about 1.1 billion to 750 million years ago, long before Pangaea?
giai_thich: The name Rodinia comes from the Russian word "rodina," meaning "homeland," because it is believed that all subsequent continents originated from it. Rodinia broke apart about 750 million years ago; this breakup may be related to the "Snowball Earth" events. Before Rodinia, there were even older supercontinents like Columbia (Nuna). Continents seem to come together into supercontinents and then break apart in cycles of about 400-600 million years.

cau_hoi: According to geologists, in about 200-250 million years, the continents may merge into a new supercontinent. What is one of the proposed names for that future supercontinent?
giai_thich: There are several scenarios: if the Pacific Ocean closes, America will collide with Asia, forming "Amasia" (a blend of America and Asia). If the Atlantic Ocean closes, "Pangaea Proxima" (the next Pangaea) may form. A simulation in 2023 suggested that the future supercontinent could be too hot and dry, making it difficult for most mammals to survive.

cau_hoi: What is the name of the ancient ocean that lay between Gondwana and Laurasia, of which the remnants today are part of the Mediterranean?
giai_thich: Tethys is named after the sea goddess in Greek mythology. As Africa and India drifted northward and collided with Europe and Asia, the Tethys Ocean gradually closed, its seabed being uplifted into the Alps and Himalayas. This is why many marine fossils are found in these mountain ranges. Panthalassa was the vast ocean surrounding Pangaea, the precursor to the Pacific Ocean.

cau_hoi: What do climatologists study by measuring the ratio of oxygen-18 to oxygen-16 in ice cores and small marine organism shells to learn about the past?
A: The rotation speed of the Earth
D: The temperature and ice volume on Earth in ancient times
giai_thich: Water containing oxygen-16 is lighter and evaporates more easily. In cold climates, much of the lighter water gets trapped in large ice sheets, making ocean water richer in oxygen-18, and the shells of marine organisms (like foraminifera) also record that ratio. In ice cores, the isotope ratio of snow indicates the temperature at the time the snow fell. Thanks to this "isotope thermometer," we know about the climate millions of years ago.

cau_hoi: Why do scientists study the "Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum" (PETM) that occurred about 56 million years ago?
A: It was the coldest time on Earth
C: A large amount of carbon was released into the atmosphere causing the Earth to warm by about 5 – 8°C, similar to a "test" for today's climate change
D: It was when the Moon formed
giai_thich: Over a few thousand years, trillions of tons of carbon, possibly from volcanoes or burning ice at the ocean floor, entered the atmosphere and oceans. The oceans became acidic, many deep-sea organisms went extinct, and land mammals shrank and migrated to polar regions. The concerning fact is that humans are currently releasing carbon much faster than during the PETM.

cau_hoi: What was the "Younger Dryas" event, which occurred about 12,900 – 11,700 years ago?
A: The formation of the Sahara Desert
B: A sudden cold snap lasting about 1,200 years, just as the Earth was emerging from the ice age
giai_thich: As the climate was warming, the Northern Hemisphere suddenly cooled back to near ice age conditions within a few decades. The popular hypothesis is that fresh water from Lake Agassiz flowed into the North Atlantic, weakening the heat-carrying ocean current. The name comes from the flower Dryas octopetala, which was abundant in the sediments of this period.

cau_hoi: During the "Little Ice Age" (approximately the 14th to 19th centuries), there were winters when the Thames River in London froze thickly. What did people do on the river?
A: Held a "Frost Fair" with stalls, games, and even an elephant walking on the ice
giai_thich: This period was colder than usual in Europe and North America, possibly due to numerous volcanic eruptions and reduced solar activity. The last Frost Fair on the Thames took place in 1814, where an elephant was led across the ice. After that, the old London Bridge was replaced, and the water flowed faster, making it harder for the river to freeze again. Winter paintings by Dutch artists also depict this frigid period.

cau_hoi: In the early 20th century, British scientist Gilbert Walker discovered the "Southern Oscillation." What is it?
A: The oscillation of tides in the Southern Hemisphere
C: The change in salinity of the Southern Ocean
D: The back-and-forth oscillation of air pressure between the western and eastern tropical Pacific, closely related to El Niño
giai_thich: Walker was working in India, trying to forecast the monsoon after a devastating famine. He noticed that when the pressure in Darwin (Australia) was high, the pressure in Tahiti was low, and vice versa. It wasn't until the 1960s that meteorologist Jacob Bjerknes pointed out that the Southern Oscillation and El Niño are two sides of the same phenomenon, now collectively referred to as ENSO.

cau_hoi: Why is a "supercell" a particularly dangerous type of thunderstorm?
B: It contains a continuously rotating updraft (mesocyclone), which can produce strong tornadoes and very large hail
giai_thich: When winds at different altitudes blow in different directions and speeds, the updraft in the thunderstorm gets twisted into a rotating column several kilometers wide. Supercells can last for hours, causing most strong tornadoes, large hail, and severe gusty winds. From a distance, they can look like a giant rotating spaceship.

cau_hoi: On weather radar, a rain band that curves into a "hook shape" at the edge of a thunderstorm usually warns of what?
A: The cloud is about to dissipate
C: A tornado may be occurring or about to occur
D: A rainbow is about to appear
giai_thich: The hook shape appears when rain is wrapped around the rotating updraft of a supercell. This sign was first recognized in 1953 in Illinois (USA). Today, Doppler radar can also measure the wind speed moving towards or away from the radar, allowing for direct detection of rotation, helping to warn of tornadoes about 10 – 15 minutes earlier.

cau_hoi: "Derecho" is what kind of weather phenomenon?
A: A very long line of thunderstorms moving quickly, causing straight-line winds as strong as a hurricane over distances of hundreds of kilometers
giai_thich: Unlike tornadoes with rotating winds, derechos produce winds blowing in one direction, which can exceed 150 km/h, sweeping across hundreds of kilometers. The name in Spanish means "straight." In 2020, a derecho in Iowa (USA) flattened millions of hectares of corn and caused billions of dollars in damage, one of the most damaging thunderstorms in U.S. history.

cau_hoi: "Haboob" is the name of what phenomenon, commonly encountered in Sudan, the Middle East, and the Arizona desert (USA)?
B: A massive wall of dust and sand pushed by a cold downdraft from a thunderstorm
giai_thich: When thunderstorms form over the desert, cold air descends rapidly from the cloud, spreading out across the ground and lifting dust and sand into a towering wall that can reach over 1 km high, moving at tens of km/h. The name comes from Arabic, meaning "to blow strongly." Haboobs can reduce visibility to near zero and may cause airports to close.

cau_hoi: "Bomb cyclone" is a meteorological term for what phenomenon?
A: A low-pressure area that intensifies extremely quickly, with pressure at the center dropping at least about 24 hPa in 24 hours
B: A storm created by a bomb
C: A storm that only occurs during war
giai_thich: The term was popularized by meteorologists Fred Sanders and John Gyakum in 1980. Such rapid pressure drops cause winds to suddenly intensify. Bomb cyclones typically form in winter off the eastern coast of North America or Japan, when cold continental air meets warm ocean currents, causing severe snowstorms. The name sounds frightening but has nothing to do with real bombs.

cau_hoi: Scientists warn that a wet bulb temperature (a combination of temperature and humidity) of about 35°C is considered a dangerous limit. Why?
A: Because at that level the Sun stops shining
B: Because at that level the air runs out of oxygen
C: At this level, sweating can hardly cool the body; even healthy people resting in the shade can be in danger after a few hours
D: Because at that level water boils
giai_thich: Wet bulb temperature is measured with a thermometer wrapped in wet cloth, indicating how much the air can cool by evaporation. When it reaches skin temperature of about 35°C, the body cannot dissipate heat. Recent studies suggest the actual limit is even lower, around 31°C for many people. Some areas near the Persian Gulf and South Asia have recorded times close to this.

cau_hoi: In 2011, the KamLAND experiment in Japan detected "geoneutrinos" emitted from the Earth's interior. What does this indicate about the planet's internal heat source?
A: All heat comes from the Sun
B: The Earth's core is undergoing nuclear fusion like the Sun
C: The Earth is completely no longer hot
D: About half of the heat escaping from the Earth's interior comes from the radioactive decay of uranium, thorium, and potassium
giai_thich: The Earth emits about 44 – 47 trillion watts of heat from within. Part of this is residual heat from when the Earth formed, and the rest comes from decaying radioactive elements. As uranium and thorium decay, they emit neutrinos that pass through the entire planet; the KamLAND detector, located deep underground, has "caught" them, allowing for the first direct measurement of radioactive heat.

cau_hoi: In 2014, scientists found a diamond from deep within the mantle containing water-bearing ringwoodite. What does this discovery suggest?
A: The Earth's core is made of ice
C: At depths of about 410 – 660 km, there may be an amount of water equivalent to or greater than all the oceans, locked in rock
D: There is an underground ocean of liquid water with fish living in it
giai_thich: Ringwoodite is a mineral that is stable only under very high pressure in the mantle's "transition zone" and can hold water in its crystal structure. The small diamond found in Brazil containing ringwoodite has about 1.5% of its mass as water. If the entire transition zone has a similar amount of water, it would be a massive "ocean" locked in rock rather than liquid water.

cau_hoi: How did the January 2022 underwater volcanic eruption of Hunga Tonga – Hunga Haʻapai differ from other major eruptions in terms of climate impact?
A: Doubled the thickness of the ozone layer
B: Erupted a massive amount of water vapor into the stratosphere, increasing the water vapor there by about 10%
C: Caused the Earth to cool significantly for many years
D: Did not eject anything into the sky
giai_thich: Because the volcano is underwater, the explosion pushed about 146 million tons of water into the stratosphere, reaching over 50 km high, the highest plume ever recorded. Water vapor is a greenhouse gas, so it may temporarily warm the Earth instead of cooling it as most eruptions do. The pressure waves from the explosion circled the Earth multiple times and were recorded by sensors worldwide.

cau_hoi: "Terra preta" (black earth) in the Amazon basin, unusually fertile compared to surrounding soil, was formed how?
D: By ancient indigenous people creating it with charcoal, pottery shards, bones, and organic waste
giai_thich: Amazon rainforest soil is often nutrient-poor due to leaching from rain. However, terra preta areas, sometimes up to 2 m deep, are rich in biochar that retains nutrients and microorganisms very well, remaining fertile for hundreds of years. This discovery indicates that the Amazon once had dense populations, not just wilderness. Today, people are learning from this method to improve soil.

cau_hoi: In 1958, America's first satellite, Explorer 1, helped discover what around the Earth?
A: Radiation belts (Van Allen belts) containing charged particles trapped by the magnetic field
giai_thich: The Geiger counter on Explorer 1, designed by James Van Allen's team, sometimes recorded zero particles in a strange way. Van Allen understood that the device had been "saturated" due to too many particles. This was evidence of high-energy particle belts trapped by the Earth's magnetic field. Today, spacecraft must pass through the belts quickly or be shielded to protect equipment and people.

cau_hoi: Since 1972, a "leap second" has occasionally been added to world clocks. Why is this necessary?
B: Because leap years lack a second
C: Because the Earth's rotation is uneven and tends to slow down, so atomic time must be adjusted to match the position of the Sun
D: Because the Moon is moving closer
giai_thich: Atomic clocks are extremely stable, but the Earth is not: tidal forces slow it down, and the movement of the core, melting ice, and earthquakes also slightly change the rotation speed. So far, 27 leap seconds have been added. Because leap seconds cause issues for computers and the Internet, scientists decided to eliminate leap seconds before 2035.

cau_hoi: How have the two GRACE satellites flying in tandem (since 2002) helped scientists "weigh" changes in water on Earth?
C: By taking color photographs of water
D: By measuring tiny changes in the distance between the two satellites due to varying gravity in each region
giai_thich: When a region gains mass, such as an increase in groundwater, gravity there is slightly stronger, pulling the leading satellite faster before the trailing satellite arrives. By measuring the distance between the two satellites with micrometer precision, scientists can calculate how much ice is lost each year in Greenland and Antarctica and how groundwater in India and California is depleting.

cau_hoi: What is the main reason many areas of Ho Chi Minh City, Jakarta, or Bangkok are sinking several centimeters each year?
B: Over-extraction of groundwater causing soil layers to compress
D: The Moon pulling the land down
giai_thich: When groundwater is pumped out, clay and sand layers lose water, compressing like a squeezed sponge, and the ground sinks, often unable to recover. The weight of high-rise buildings on weak ground also contributes. In some areas, the sinking rate is even faster than the sea level rise, significantly increasing the risk of flooding. Jakarta is sinking so fast that Indonesia has decided to build a new capital.

cau_hoi: According to the Global Volcanism Program (Smithsonian), how many volcanoes on land are considered potentially active (having erupted in the last 12,000 years)?
giai_thich: About 50 – 70 volcanoes erupt each year, and at any given time, about 20 volcanoes are erupting. This number does not include the majority of underwater volcanoes, especially along mid-ocean ridges, where there may be thousands of unstudied volcanoes. Indonesia has the most active volcanoes, while the U.S. ranks second in total number.

cau_hoi: In December 2018, a tsunami unexpectedly hit the shores of the Sunda Strait (Indonesia) without any prior earthquake warning. What was the cause?
B: A part of the Anak Krakatau volcano collapsed into the sea
D: A meteorite fell into the sea
giai_thich: Anak Krakatau ("Child of Krakatoa") emerged from the old Krakatoa volcano's mouth in 1927. In 2018, during an eruption, its southwestern flank collapsed into the sea, displacing water and generating a tsunami that killed over 400 people. Since the warning system primarily relies on earthquakes, tsunamis caused by volcanic collapses are very difficult to detect early. After the collapse, the volcano's height decreased by about two-thirds.

cau_hoi: What was the highest wind speed ever recorded near the ground in a tornado, measured by mobile Doppler radar in 1999 in Oklahoma (USA)?
giai_thich: The Bridge Creek – Moore tornado on May 3, 1999, was measured by a "Doppler on wheels" radar to have winds of about 484 km/h at a height of several dozen meters, faster than the fastest speedboat. The tornado destroyed thousands of homes. It is very difficult to measure wind in a tornado because measuring devices are often destroyed, so scientists have to drive radar vehicles close to "hunt" the tornado.

cau_hoi: At a depth of about 660 km in the mantle, seismic waves suddenly travel faster. What is the reason?
A: Pressure causes the mineral ringwoodite to transform into bridgmanite and denser minerals
B: It is the boundary with the Earth's core
D: There is a layer of liquid water there
giai_thich: Rocks do not change composition, but their crystal structure changes as pressure increases, similar to how carbon can become graphite or diamond. At about 660 km, the atoms in ringwoodite rearrange more tightly into bridgmanite and ferropericlase, making the rock denser and the waves travel faster. This boundary also affects whether oceanic plates can sink through or get "stuck".

cau_hoi: About 500 – 420 million years ago, an ancient ocean separated the land that is now Scotland from the land that is now England. What was the name of that ocean?
giai_thich: Iapetus was named after the father of Atlas in Greek mythology, as it was the "precursor" to the Atlantic Ocean. When this ocean closed, the continental blocks collided, forming the Caledonian mountain range, which is now the mountains of Scotland, Norway, and part of the Appalachian range. The sutured boundary of the ancient ocean runs near the present-day England-Scotland border.

cau_hoi: In 1902, Swedish scientist Vagn Walfrid Ekman explained why icebergs do not drift in the direction of the wind but shift to the right. What does "Ekman transport" describe?
A: Sea water flows according to the Moon
C: Due to the Earth's rotation, the surface water pushed by the wind moves about 90° off the wind direction (to the right in the Northern Hemisphere)
D: Ocean waves always run against the wind
giai_thich: Explorer Fridtjof Nansen noticed that icebergs drifted off the wind direction and asked Ekman for an explanation. Each layer of water drags the layer below, and the Coriolis force gradually rotates the direction of movement with depth into a spiral. In summary, water moves perpendicular to the wind. This is why winds blowing along the coasts of Peru and California push surface water offshore, allowing cold, nutrient-rich water to rise.

cau_hoi: "Madden – Julian Oscillation" (MJO), discovered in 1971, is what phenomenon?
A: An ocean current in the Arctic
B: A large area of rain clouds moving slowly from the Indian Ocean eastward across the Pacific, repeating approximately every 30 – 60 days
giai_thich: MJO is like a "wave" of rain and wind circling the tropics. As it passes, it increases rainfall in one area and decreases it in another, affecting the onset of monsoons, the formation of tropical storms, and even El Niño. Because it has a cycle of several weeks, MJO helps meteorologists forecast weather beyond the usual limit of about 10 days.

cau_hoi: "North Atlantic Oscillation" (NAO) strongly affects winter in Europe. When the NAO index is strongly positive, how is winter in Northern Europe typically?
A: Warmer and wetter due to strong westerly winds bringing ocean air in
giai_thich: NAO measures the pressure difference between the Icelandic low and the Azores high. When the difference is large (positive NAO), strong westerly winds bring warm, moist storms from the Atlantic into Northern Europe, while Southern Europe becomes drier. When NAO is negative, westerly winds weaken, allowing cold air from the Arctic and Siberia to spill down, leading to bitterly cold winters in Europe like in 2010.

cau_hoi: "Indian Ocean Dipole" (IOD) occurs when, and what does it usually affect?
A: Tides in the Indian Ocean are twice as strong
C: The sea water across the Indian Ocean freezes
D: The sea water in the western Indian Ocean is warmer than in the east, causing heavy rains in East Africa and droughts in Australia and Indonesia
giai_thich: IOD is like the "brother" of El Niño in the Indian Ocean, described by Japanese and Indian scientists in 1999. In 2019, a very strong positive IOD contributed to severe drought in Australia, creating conditions for the "Black Summer" bushfire season, while causing flooding in East Africa.

cau_hoi: Where is the upper boundary of the troposphere (the top of the troposphere) located, which is the coldest place at about −80°C, even though it is above the hottest surface area?
giai_thich: At the equator, hot air rises very strongly, pushing the top of the troposphere up to about 16 – 18 km. Because the temperature decreases uniformly with height in the troposphere, the top at the equator is much colder than at the poles (the top is only about 8 km high, around −50°C). This very cold layer of air "dries out" moisture, making the stratosphere above extremely dry.

cau_hoi: In 2019, scientists announced that a rock sample brought back from the Moon by Apollo 14 (called "Big Bertha") could be what?
C: An ancient rock fragment from Earth, about 4 billion years old, that was ejected to the Moon by a collision
D: A piece of metal left by aliens
giai_thich: The small rock contains minerals like quartz and zircon, formed at temperatures and depths more similar to Earth's crust than the Moon. Scientists believe that about 4 billion years ago, when the Moon was much closer to Earth, a meteorite collision ejected this rock fragment to the Moon. If true, it is one of the oldest rock fragments of Earth ever found, and it is located on the Moon.

cau_hoi: "The faint young Sun paradox," proposed by Carl Sagan and George Mullen in 1972, raises what question?
A: Why did the early Earth have liquid water even though the Sun was about 30% dimmer than today?
B: Why doesn't the Sun burn out?
C: Why is the Moon brighter than the Sun?
giai_thich: According to stellar theory, the young Sun was much weaker, and the Earth should have frozen for about the first 2 billion years. However, ancient rocks show that liquid water and life existed very early. The common explanation is that the primordial atmosphere contained a lot of greenhouse gases like CO₂ and methane, retaining heat more effectively than today. A completely unified solution has yet to be found.

cau_hoi: Geologists mark the official boundary between geological periods at a specific rock layer at a location in the world, commonly referred to as what?
B: "Golden spike" (GSSP – Global Standard Stratotype and Point)
giai_thich: To unify the world on where an era begins, the International Commission on Stratigraphy selects a representative rock section and drives a spike (usually made of copper) into the exact boundary layer. For example, the boundary between the Cretaceous and Paleogene periods (when dinosaurs went extinct) is marked at El Kef, Tunisia. Currently, about 80 "golden spikes" have been placed around the world.

cau_hoi: In 2018, the Holocene epoch was divided into three phases. The current phase, which began about 4,200 years ago with a major drought, is named after a state in India. What is this phase called?
giai_thich: The time marker is determined by stalagmite layers in Mawmluh Cave in Meghalaya, recording a drought about 4,200 years ago, which may have contributed to the decline of many civilizations like Akkad in Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley civilization. The two previous phases are the Greenland phase (based on the Greenland ice core) and the Northgrip phase. This is the first time a geological time unit has been named after a location in India.

cau_hoi: "Chandler wobble," discovered by American amateur astronomer Seth Chandler in 1891, is what phenomenon?
A: The Sun changes color with the seasons
B: The Earth's rotation axis wobbles slightly relative to the ground, with the pole's position shifting a few meters in a cycle of about 433 days
D: The Moon oscillates up and down
giai_thich: The Earth is not a perfect solid sphere, so its rotation axis wobbles like a top, causing the geographic North Pole to trace small circles with a diameter of about 6 – 9 m on the Arctic ice. This wobble should have diminished, but it persists, possibly due to pressure changes at the ocean floor and in the atmosphere. Accurate positioning systems must account for this phenomenon.

cau_hoi: The WGS 84 coordinate system used by phones and GPS worldwide describes the Earth as what shape?
C: An oblate spheroid slightly flattened at the poles, with the equatorial diameter about 43 km greater than the polar diameter
giai_thich: Due to its rotation, the Earth bulges at the equator. The equatorial radius is about 6,378 km, while the polar radius is about 6,357 km. WGS 84 was developed by the U.S. Department of Defense in 1984 and has been updated multiple times. Each country's maps, such as Vietnam's VN-2000 system, may use a more suitable ellipsoid for their region, so coordinate transformations must be considered when switching between them.

cau_hoi: InSAR technology, using radar from satellites, helps scientists measure what?
A: The number of fish in the sea
B: The temperature of the Earth's core
D: Changes in ground elevation of just a few millimeters over large areas, such as land subsidence or volcanic uplift
giai_thich: Satellites capture radar images of the same area at different times. By comparing the "phase" of the reflected radar waves, scientists can map color patterns showing how much the ground has risen or fallen. This allows them to detect volcanoes "inflating" before eruption, measure how earthquakes shift the ground, and monitor land subsidence in cities.

cau_hoi: Darcy's law (1856), discovered by French engineer Henry Darcy while designing a water supply system for the city of Dijon, describes what?
B: The flow rate of water through porous rock is proportional to the pressure difference and the permeability of the rock
giai_thich: Darcy allowed water to flow through columns of sand and measured the amount of water that flowed out. He found that the flow rate increased when the difference in water level between the two ends was greater and when the sand was coarser and more permeable. This simple law became the foundation of groundwater hydrology, oil and gas extraction, and even coffee brewing research. The unit of permeability "darcy" is named after him.

cau_hoi: Seismologists found that seismic waves travel through the Earth's inner core faster in the north-south direction than in the direction parallel to the equator. How is this phenomenon primarily explained?
A: Because there is water in the core
B: Because the Moon pulls the inner core
C: Because the inner core is hollow in the middle
D: Iron crystals in the inner core are aligned in a preferred direction
giai_thich: This phenomenon is called the anisotropy of the inner core, discovered since the 1980s. Similar to wood splitting along the grain, the alignment of iron crystals in a certain direction causes waves to travel faster in that direction, with a difference of about 3%. In 2023, scientists also found signs of a "inner inner core" about 650 km wide, where the crystal alignment is completely different.

cau_hoi: "The Bergeron – Findeisen process," the main cause of rain in temperate regions, occurs how?
A: Winds push clouds together to create rain
B: Water droplets collide and stick together
C: In cold clouds, there are both ice crystals and supercooled water droplets, with ice crystals growing rapidly by "taking" water vapor from the droplets
giai_thich: At temperatures below 0°C, water vapor is more likely to adhere to ice than to liquid water. Therefore, in a cloud containing both, water droplets gradually evaporate while ice crystals grow quickly, becoming heavy enough to fall, melting into rain when passing through warm air. In tropical regions, warm clouds primarily produce rain by droplets colliding and merging.

cau_hoi: In clouds, water can exist in liquid form at temperatures as low as about what without freezing?
giai_thich: Pure water needs a "nucleus" like a dust particle or ice crystal to start freezing. Tiny water droplets in clouds, lacking a nucleus, can remain liquid at very low temperatures, known as supercooled water. When an airplane flies through clouds with supercooled water, the droplets freeze instantly upon contact with the wings, creating dangerous ice buildup. Therefore, airplanes have anti-icing systems on their wings.

cau_hoi: When a dry air mass rises, how much does its temperature decrease per kilometer due to expansion?
giai_thich: This is the "dry adiabatic lapse rate". If the air is saturated with water vapor, the water vapor condenses as it rises and releases heat, so it cools more slowly, about 5 – 6°C per km. This difference explains foehn winds: moist air rising over mountains cools more slowly and loses moisture as rain, then heats up quickly on the other side according to the dry lapse rate, becoming hot dry winds.

cau_hoi: "Chapman Cycle" (1930), proposed by British physicist Sydney Chapman, explains what?
A: Water cycling between the sea and land
C: Carbon cycling between organisms and the atmosphere
D: Ozone is continuously created and destroyed in the stratosphere under the influence of ultraviolet rays
giai_thich: Strong ultraviolet rays split oxygen molecules (O₂) into two oxygen atoms; each atom combines with another O₂ molecule to form ozone (O₃). Ozone absorbs ultraviolet rays and is broken down. This balanced cycle keeps the ozone layer stable. Later, scientists discovered substances like chlorine from CFCs could break down ozone much faster than the natural cycle.

cau_hoi: A 2016 study suggested that the oldest remaining oceanic crust on Earth, about 340 million years old, could be located where?
B: In the middle of the Pacific Ocean
giai_thich: Most ocean floors are not older than 200 million years due to subduction. However, geophysicist Roi Granot analyzed magnetic stripes beneath thick sediment in the Herodotus Basin (eastern Mediterranean) and suggested this could be a remnant of the ancient Tethys Ocean, formed when the supercontinent Pangaea was still forming. This conclusion is still debated.

cau_hoi: In 1862, physicist Lord Kelvin estimated the age of the Earth based on its cooling rate and came up with a result of about 20 – 400 million years. Why was his estimate so far off?
B: He was unaware of radioactivity, an additional heat source inside the Earth, and assumed the Earth cooled like a solid mass
C: Because he used the wrong unit of measurement
D: Because he calculated according to the Bible
giai_thich: Kelvin viewed the Earth as a cooling molten sphere, only radiating heat outward. The short result worried geologists and Darwin because it did not allow enough time for evolution. Radioactivity was discovered in 1896, showing that the Earth's interior had an additional heat source. Additionally, the convective mantle also brings heat from deep inside, helping the surface retain heat much longer.

cau_hoi: In 1913, which young British geologist wrote the book "The Age of the Earth", pioneering the use of radioactivity to determine rock ages, estimating the Earth to be at least 1.6 billion years old?
giai_thich: Arthur Holmes measured the ratio of uranium to lead in minerals to calculate rock ages when he was only about 23 years old. He was also one of the first to support the idea of convection in the mantle to explain continental drift. His textbook "Principles of Physical Geology" was widely used for decades. His estimates of the Earth's age gradually increased to about 4.5 billion years by the 1950s.

cau_hoi: Some historians call the year 536 the "worst year to be alive". What was the main reason?
A: A major volcanic eruption (possibly in Iceland) covered Europe, the Middle East, and Asia with dust fog, causing a cold snap and crop failures
C: A meteorite destroyed the city of Rome
giai_thich: In 536, Byzantine historian Procopius wrote that the Sun shone dimly like the Moon all year. The summer was cold, snow fell in China, and crops failed. Ice cores show a major eruption occurred in 536, and another in 540. Shortly after, in 541, the Justinian plague broke out. This marked the beginning of a cold period lasting over a century.

cau_hoi: About 2.4 – 2.1 billion years ago, the Earth experienced the "Huronian Glaciation", one of the longest ice ages. What is believed to be the cause?
A: The Earth was pushed away from the Sun by a meteorite
B: Increased oxygen destroyed methane, a potent greenhouse gas, in the atmosphere
giai_thich: This was the time when cyanobacteria began to enrich the atmosphere with oxygen. Oxygen reacted with methane, a crucial greenhouse gas at that time due to the weak Sun, converting it into CO₂, which retains heat less effectively. The greenhouse effect weakened, and the Earth plunged into ice for possibly hundreds of millions of years. The name comes from glacial sediment layers around Lake Huron in Canada.

cau_hoi: Scientists identified an earthquake of about 9 degrees in the Cascadia subduction zone (West Coast of North America) that occurred on the evening of January 26, 1700, based on what evidence?
C: Japanese records of a "solitary" tsunami that struck without any felt earthquake
giai_thich: At that time, North America had no written records, but indigenous legends spoke of a great shaking. Scientists found stumps of cedar trees killed by subsidence due to saltwater intrusion, and tree rings indicated they died around 1699 – 1700. Records in Japan noted a tsunami on January 27 – 28, 1700, without any earthquake felt in Japan, helping to backtrack to the exact timing.

cau_hoi: "Atmospheric window" in the infrared wavelength range of 8 – 13 micrometers plays what role in Earth's climate?
A: It is where visible light is blocked
B: It is the wavelength range where thermal radiation from the ground escapes into space easily because it is less absorbed by the atmosphere
C: It is a hole in the ozone layer
D: It is where radio waves are reflected
giai_thich: Most of the Earth's heat radiates in the infrared range, but water vapor and CO₂ strongly absorb at many wavelengths. The range of 8 – 13 micrometers is relatively "transparent", like a window for heat to escape; this is why clear nights are often colder. Some gases emitted by humans, like CFCs, absorb precisely in this window, making each molecule of them hold heat very effectively.

cau_hoi: In 2012, an earthquake of about 8.6 degrees off the coast of Sumatra surprised scientists for what reason?
A: It made the Earth stop spinning
B: It did not generate any seismic waves
C: It occurred on land in Europe
D: It was the strongest strike-slip earthquake ever recorded, occurring within a plate rather than at a plate boundary
giai_thich: Most of the largest earthquakes occur at subduction zones. The earthquake on April 11, 2012, in the Indian Ocean was caused by strike-slip faults located within the Indo-Australian Plate, and it also triggered many other faults. Scientists believe the Indo-Australian Plate is gradually splitting into two plates. Being a strike-slip earthquake, it only generated small tsunamis.
